reasoning: The defect is real. duckdb_vector_get_validity is typed uint64(intp) at ducklib.py:236, but the DuckDB C API declares it as `uint64_t *duckdb_vector_get_validity(duckdb_vector vector)` — a pointer return, not a scalar. The all-pointers-are-intp convention is clearly established in numbox (signatures.py: all stdio/string/memory C functions use intp for every pointer), in CLAUDE.md, and consistently followed throughout ducklib.py itself: the sibling duckdb_vector_get_data (void*) is correctly typed intp(intp) at line 235. The type mismatch with duckdb_validity_row_is_valid is also real: that function's first argument (uint64_t *validity) is correctly typed intp at line 233, so a chain duckdb_validity_row_is_valid(duckdb_vector_get_validity(v), row) in @njit code would pass a uint64 where intp (int64) is expected, requiring an implicit uint64->int64 cast. An independent review unit (DCK-sig-COR.json finding DCK-sig-COR-2) independently identified the same defect with the same recommendation. However, the medium severity is overstated. On every supported 64-bit platform (Linux x86-64, macOS ARM64, Windows x64) both uint64 and intp are 64-bit values and the pointer passes through RAX intact — ABI is fully preserved. Heap allocations never have bit 63 set on any current OS, so the uint64->int64 reinterpretation cannot corrupt the address. The worst-case observable symptom is a numba TypingError in @njit code that chains the two functions without an explicit cast — a compile-time failure rather than a silent data corruption. The existing tests call both functions from Python (where type coercion is implicit) and pass. The independent reviewer (DCK-sig-COR-2) rated the identical defect low: 'ABI-neutral ... type-hygiene/convention deviation.' Low is the correct severity.
